newsitem.title: CHINA: China to issue bonds for huge Three Gorges project.
newsitem.headline: China to issue bonds for huge Three Gorges project.

text.p: China plans to issue one billion yuan ($120 million) worth of three and five-year bonds in November to help finance construction of the huge Three Gorges project, the Xinhua news agency said on Sunday.
Xinhua gave no further details of the planned bond issue.
The Yangtze Three Gorges Development Corp would issue more bonds and possibly shares in 1997, Xinhua quoted Yuan Guolin, assistant general manager of the company, as saying.
"Construction of the Three Gorges project has been going smoothly since 1993," Yuan said.
Spending on the project reached 17 billion yuan ($2.0 billion) by August. The project is scheduled to dam the Yangtze river by the end of next year.
The $30 billion Three Gorges -- the world's biggest water control project -- was scheduled to be completed in 2009.
Xinhua quoted Yuan as telling a group of visitors from Hong Kong that the project would need more investment from the British colony, which is due to revert to Chinese rule in 1997.
"We will further tap the role of Hong Kong as an international financial centre in our fund-raising activities and hope Hong Kong investors will make investment in the project," Yuan said.
A number of of Hong Kong companies had already invested in the dam and nearby areas, Xinhua said, without giving further details.

The project will create a huge reservoir and is expected to reduce flooding along the 6,000-km (3,500-mile) Yangtze, China's longest river, and to provide an additional 85 million megawatt hours of electricity per year.

The controversial project will submerge 632 square km (244 square miles) of land in Hubei province in central China and the southwestern province of Sichuan, forcing the relocation of nearly one million residents of up to 200 towns and villages.
Chinese and foreign environmentalists have criticised the project, describing it as a potential environmental disaster.
The U.S. Export-Import Bank has rejected a request from U.S. companies to provide financial backing for the project, citing environmental concerns.
Many local residents have objected to the forced relocation and complained of inadequate compensation.
